key_concept: Conjugated double bonds alternate with exactly one single bond ($C=C-C=C$), so the two locants of a conjugated diene differ by 2.
steps: Recall the classification of dienes. Cumulated dienes have adjacent double bonds ($C=C=C$). Conjugated dienes have double bonds separated by one single bond ($C=C-C=C$). Isolated dienes have double bonds separated by two or more single bonds.
Hepta-1,3-diene is $CH_2=CH-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3$. The double bonds are $C1=C2$ and $C3=C4$, separated only by the single bond $C2-C3$. This is conjugated.
Hepta-1,4-diene is $CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_3$. An $sp^3$ $CH_2$ group (C3) lies between the double bonds. This is isolated.
Hepta-1,5-diene is $CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH=CH-CH_3$. Two $CH_2$ groups separate the double bonds. This is isolated.
Hepta-1,6-diene is $CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH=CH_2$. Three $CH_2$ groups separate the double bonds. This is isolated.
Only hepta-1,3-diene has the alternating pattern, so its $p$-orbitals overlap continuously across $C1$ to $C4$.
why_not_others: In the 1,4-, 1,5- and 1,6-dienes, at least one $sp^3$ $CH_2$ carbon lies between the double bonds. This breaks the continuous $p$-orbital overlap, so these double bonds are isolated, not conjugated.
common_trap: Students sometimes confuse conjugated dienes (locant difference of 2) with cumulated dienes (locant difference of 1, as in allene). Others think any diene with nearby double bonds is conjugated.
time_saving_tip: Subtract the locants. A difference of 1 means cumulated, 2 means conjugated, and more than 2 means isolated. Here only $3-1=2$.
